newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Malaysia tells Australia of race row offence.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia tells Australia of race row offence.

text.p: Regional concern over Australia's heated race debate has intensified, with Malaysia expressing official concern about an apparent rise in anti-Asian feeling.
Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi said he had told his Australian counterpart Alexander Downer in Manila on Thursday that the issue was causing offence in Malaysia.
It is the first time an Asian government has raised the row, raging since September, at ministerial level.
"I think this is a big issue, it is also a big issue in Malaysia and we feel somewhat offended," Badawi told Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) radio in an interview broadcast on Friday.

Badawi rejected claims by some Australian politicians, including senior figures in the Liberal-National government, that the race debate was not hitting Australia's relations with its key Asian neighbours.
"I think they are making a wrong reading of this, I think that shows that they don't understand us," he said.
Asked about the impact of the debate on relations, Badawi said: "Well, first, we get a feeling that Australians are not going to be friendly with us, and that's bad.
"We already have a history of hiccups in our bilateral relations and when this is done we can't help getting that kind of feeling."
Outspoken independent politician Pauline Hanson sparked the row in September with a parliamentary speech warning Asians were swamping Australia and urging a halt to immigration.
Her comments and the race and immigration debate they sparked have been blamed for a rise in official complaints about racism and reports of increased abuse of Asians on Australia's streets.
Badawi said Downer had distanced the government from remarks by any group "that have been resorting to or saying things which show that they are anti-Asian".
Downer told the ABC he had assured Badawi the government abhorred racism.
"We've all gone out of our way to make it absolutely clear that we totally repudiate racist sentiments, that Australia is a tolerant society," he said.
"I wouldn't say that it (racism) was an issue that was in the broad going to damage Australia's long-term interests."

Relations between Australia and Malaysia have been rocky through the 1990s. Malaysia was angered by former prime minister Paul Keating's description of Malaysian leader Mahathir Mohamad as a "recalcitrant" in 1993.
Criticism from Australian human rights and conservation groups and an Australian television seen by Kuala Lumur as damaging have also affected relations.
